metric_rationale: This metric evaluates the proportion of trials where the subject's choice aligns with the Take The Best (TTB) prediction. Because the experimental design explicitly pits TTB against Tallying (creating multiple trials where the highest valid cue points to one option, but a larger number of lower-validity cues point to the other), TTB simulated data will score near 1.0 on this metric. Conversely, Tallying simulated data will systematically choose the opposite option on the mismatch trials, scoring very low (close to 0.0 or 0.1). This creates a massive, reliable gap with low between-subject variance.

This metric calculates the proportion of subject responses that align with the deterministic prediction of the Tallying heuristic, excluding trials where Tallying predicts a tie. Because the experimental design explicitly pits Tallying against Take The Best (TTB) by including many trials where a single high-validity cue points one way while a majority of lower-validity cues point the other way, the two models make strictly opposite predictions on most trials. Consequently, data generated under Tallying will yield a high value on this metric (reflecting high agreement), whereas data generated under TTB will yield a low value (reflecting choices driven by the single highest-validity cue rather than the unweighted majority). The averaging across a large number of discriminating trials per subject ensures low within-theory variance.

This metric calculates the proportion of times the subject chooses Option A on 'compensatory' trials (Trials 1 and 2). On these trials, Option A possesses only the single highest-validity cue available, while Option B possesses all remaining lower-validity cues. The Take The Best (TTB) strategy will deterministically choose Option A because it bases its decision exclusively on the single best discriminating cue. In contrast, the Weighted Additive (WADD) strategy will aggregate the evidence from the lower-validity cues, which together outweigh the single best cue for most values of the gamma parameter, thus leading WADD to predominantly choose Option B. Consequently, this metric will be close to 1 for TTB and much closer to 0 for WADD.

On Trial 1, Option A is favored by the single best cue (validity 0.95), while Option B is favored by all other cues (validities 0.9, 0.85, 0.8, 0.75). Take The Best will deterministically choose Option A (response 0) because it only considers the first discriminating cue. Weighted Additive, on the other hand, will integrate all cues and, for most values of gamma, strongly favor Option B (response 1) because the sum of the remaining validities outweighs the first. Measuring the proportion of B choices on this specific trial provides a highly stable and strongly discriminative metric between the two theories.
